title: Rust: ownership and borrowing
summary: Each value has one owner; moving it, lending it with & or &mut, and why rustc refuses some loans.

scheme: let s = String::from("hi");  s owns it
text: Every value in Rust has one owner, usually a variable. When the owner's block ends, at its }, the value is freed (dropped).
- No garbage collector, and no free() to forget: rustc places the cleanup for you.
- That's how Rust avoids the use-after-free and double-free bugs of C. Leaks stay possible (an Rc cycle), just rarer.

scheme: let b = a;           the text moves to b
text: Assigning a String, or passing it to a function, moves it: the new variable is the owner now.
- The old name can't be used anymore: rustc stops at borrow of moved value.
- Numbers and bools are copied instead (they are Copy): both names keep working.
- Need two real copies? a.clone() makes one, and costs memory.
& lends a value without moving it: it makes a reference, and that is called borrowing.
- The function reads it, the owner keeps it, and you can call it again.
- A function that only reads takes &str (text), &[T] (a list) or &T, not String or Vec.
- A borrow can't outlive the owner: rustc checks it, so no dangling pointer.

scheme: println!("{}", first); first still in use
because it is also borrowed as immutable
text: &mut lends a value to change it. At any moment you get many & or one &mut, never both.
- Here push may move the items to a bigger place: first would point at freed memory.
- The & loan lasts until first's last use: the println.
- Fix: use first before the push, or copy the number: let first = v[0];
- The same rule stops two threads from changing one value at once.
